'''Zachary David Dembo''' (born December 3, 1985) is an American politician who is the member-elect of the [[United States House of Representatives]]  from [[Kentucky's 6th congressional district]].<ref>{{cite web |title=Democrat Zach Dembo wins election to U.S. House in Kentucky's 6th Congressional District |url=https://www.kvue.com/article/syndication/associatedpress/democrat-zach-dembo-wins-election-to-us-house-in-kentuckys-6th-congressional-district/616-05db64a3-0893-4f5b-8cd0-7482880ce222 |publisher=Associated Press via KVUE |access-date=4 November 2026}}</ref>

== Early life and education ==
Dembo was born December 3, 1985, and raised in Lexington. His mother is from [[Finchville, Kentucky]], and comes from seven generations of Kentucky farmers.  His father grew up on [[Long Island]] and moved to Kentucky to teach at the [[University of Kentucky]].<ref name=":1">{{Cite web |date=June 27, 2025 |title=Zach Dembo for Congress |url=https://zachdembo.com/ |access-date=September 30, 2026 |language=en-US}}</ref>

He graduated from [[Stanford University]] in 2007 with a Bachelor of Arts in History. After university, Dembo moved to the [[Mississippi Delta]] as a corps member in the [[Teach For America]] program, where he taught 8th grade English in [[Greenville, Mississippi]], from 2007 to 2009.<ref name=":1" />

After Teach For America, Dembo enrolled in the [[University of Michigan Law School]] and received his Juris Doctor in 2012. He then commissioned into the Navy as an officer in the [[United States Navy Judge Advocate General's Corps]], where he handled a wide array of legal tasks, including helping sailors and Marines, for five years.<ref name=":1" />

==Legal career==
After receiving his honorable discharge from active duty, Dembo became a federal prosecutor at the Department of Justice in 2017, serving as a line prosecutor in the [[Civil Rights Division]] under the first Trump Administration. He served in that position until March 2020, when he accepted a position as [[Andy Beshear]]'s Policy Advisor and was then promoted to Legislative Director in 2021. He then returned to federal law enforcement as a prosecutor in the [[United States District Court for the Eastern District of Kentucky]].<ref name=":1" />

Between 2016 and 2025, he prosecuted<ref name=":3">{{Cite news |last=Cheves |first=John |date=September 21, 2026 |title=Zach Dembo prosecuted police for abuses. Is that a problem in his House race? |url=https://www.kentucky.com/news/politics-government/article317279830.html#storylink=cpy |work=Lexington Herald-Leader}}</ref> at least 38 police officers, prison, and jail guards and a juvenile detention officer accused of abusing their power, with the cases he was assigned resulting in 35 convictions and three acquittals.<ref name=":3" /> 

Dembo says he resigned from 11 years of federal service after witnessing what he described as "the corruption and politicization of the Department of Justice."<ref name=":1" />

== 2026 congressional campaign ==
Dembo announced his entry into the 6th district Democratic primary on July 17, 2025.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Staff |first=ABC 36 Digital |date=July 17, 2025 |title=Democratic and Republican candidates launch campaigns for Kentucky's 6th Congressional District |url=https://www.wtvq.com/democratic-and-republican-candidates-launch-campaigns-for-kentuckys-6th-congressional-district/ |access-date=September 30, 2026 |website=WTVQ |language=en-US}}</ref> A first time candidate, Dembo won the Democratic nomination on May 19, 2026, carrying 15 of the 16 counties in the district.<ref>{{Cite news |last=Six |first=Taylor |date=May 19, 2026 |title=Former federal prosecutor wins Democratic primary for Central KY US House seat |url=https://www.kentucky.com/news/politics-government/election/article315752541.html }}</ref>

Dembo has campaigned as a public servant who is tackling the cost of corruption he saw as a federal prosecutor in the Department of Justice before he resigned and has put out a 10-point anti-corruption plan.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Buczek |first=Karolina |date=August 25, 2026 |title=Democratic congressional candidate Zach Dembo unveils 10-point anti-corruption plan in Lexington |url=https://www.lex18.com/news/covering-kentucky/democratic-congressional-candidate-zach-dembo-unveils-10-point-anti-corruption-plan-in-lexington |access-date=September 30, 2026 |website=LEX 18 News - Lexington, KY (WLEX) |language=en}}</ref> In late April through late-May, he was endorsed by the National Education Association,<ref>{{Cite web |last=Staff |first=Web |date=May 5, 2026 |title=NEA endorses Dembo in crowded KY-06 Democratic primary |url=https://lexingtonky.news/2026/05/05/nea-endorses-dembo-in-crowded-ky-06-democratic-primary/ |access-date=September 30, 2026 |website=The Lexington Times |language=en-US}}</ref> former Lexington mayor Jim Gray,<ref>{{Cite news |last=Elam |first=Corey |date=April 22, 2026 |title=Kentucky transportation secretary, former Lexington mayor endorses Zach Dembo |url=https://fox56news.com/news/kentucky/kentucky-transportation-secretary-former-lexington-mayor-endorses-zach-dembo/ }}</ref> the last Democrat to represent the seat [[Ben Chandler]],<ref>{{Cite news |last=Horn |first=Austin |date=May 15, 2026 |title=Ben Chandler, last Democrat to hold KY-06, backs Zach Dembo for Congress |url=https://www.kentucky.com/news/politics-government/article315756916.html }}</ref> and Governor Andy Beshear,<ref>{{Cite web |last=Staff |first=WKYT News |date=June 9, 2026 |title=Beshear endorses Dembo in 6th District congressional race |url=https://www.wkyt.com/2026/06/09/beshear-endorses-dembo-6th-district-congressional-race/ |access-date=September 30, 2026 |website=www.wkyt.com |language=en}}</ref> among others. In particular, Governor Beshear took an active role in the campaign and worked closely with Dembo to flip the seat.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Sivak |first=David |date=September 19, 2026 |title=Andy Beshear goes all in to flip Trump-won House seat in Kentucky |url=https://www.washingtonexaminer.com/news/campaigns/congressional/4733711/andy-beshear-trump-house-seat-kentucky-dembo-alvarado/ |access-date=September 30, 2026 |website=Washington Examiner |language=en-US}}</ref>
